title: Nahum 2:1–7
context: The prophet warns Nineveh that the one who dashes in pieces has come up against her, and calls her to keep the fortress, watch the way, and fortify her power. The LORD restores the excellency of Jacob as the excellency of Israel, though destroyers have ruined their vine branches. An assault is described: red shields, scarlet troops, chariots like torches in the streets, picked troops dashing to the wall, the gates of the rivers opened, and the palace dissolved. The city is decreed uncovered and carried away, and her servants moan. Many readers date Nineveh’s fall to 612 BC and attribute it to a Babylonian and Median coalition; the book names Nineveh and does not give that date or those names. On the LORD’s bringing of a hostile army in judgment, see the Judges 9:23 box. Versification: English 1:15 is Hebrew 2:1, and English 2:1–13 is Hebrew 2:2–14; this page keeps the WEB numbers.

verses.text: He who dashes in pieces has come up against you. Keep the fortress! Watch the way! Strengthen your waist! Fortify your power mightily!
verses.arminianNotes:
The one who dashes in pieces has come up against Nineveh, and the city is told, “Keep the fortress! Watch the way! Strengthen your waist! Fortify your power mightily!” The calls are urgent, and they are the language of a siege already begun. The one who dashes in pieces is not named. The violence of the opening line is told in that one clause and is not described further.

Arminian readers hear a real alarm to a city that can still hear it, a coming up of a shatterer, and commands to watch and fortify that already sound too late.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the coming up of the one who dashes in pieces, and the calls to keep the fortress and fortify power, as the LORD’s appointed approach of judgment, the assault the next verses will describe.

Shared ground: a shatterer has come up, and the city is told to watch and fortify. The attacker is not named in the verse.

verses.text: For the LORD restores the excellency of Jacob as the excellency of Israel, for the destroyers have destroyed them and ruined their vine branches.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For the LORD restores the excellency of Jacob as the excellency of Israel, for the destroyers have destroyed them and ruined their vine branches.” The “for” gives the reason the assault matters: the LORD is restoring Jacob’s excellency, as Israel’s excellency, after destroyers have ruined the vine. Judah’s restoration and Nineveh’s crisis are set in one sentence.

Arminian readers hear a real restoring of a people whose vine was ruined, a goodness for Jacob that stands as the reason the shatterer is allowed to come up against the oppressor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the restoring of Jacob’s excellency, and the memory of destroyers who ruined the vine branches, as the LORD’s own purpose running through the assault.

Shared ground: the LORD restores Jacob’s excellency, and the vine had been ruined by destroyers. The verse is comfort for Israel beside the alarm for Nineveh.

verses.text: The shield of his mighty men is made red. The valiant men are in scarlet. The chariots flash with steel in the day of his preparation, and the pine spears are brandished.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The shield of his mighty men is made red. The valiant men are in scarlet. The chariots flash with steel in the day of his preparation, and the pine spears are brandished.” Shields are red, troops are in scarlet, chariots flash, spears are brandished, in the day of his preparation. Many readers take this as the army coming against Nineveh; the verse describes the preparation and does not name the army or the “his”. The picture is military, and it is given in those colors and flashes, without a longer scene.

Arminian readers hear a day of preparation already underway, a visible host whose color and steel are meant to be seen, a warning in the very look of the approaching force.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the red shields, the scarlet troops, the flashing chariots, and the brandished spears as the LORD’s appointed force in the day of preparation.

Shared ground: the army is described as ready and terrible in appearance. The owner of “his” is not named in the verse.

verses.text: The chariots rage in the streets. They rush back and forth in the wide ways. Their appearance is like torches. They run like the lightnings.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The chariots rage in the streets. They rush back and forth in the wide ways. Their appearance is like torches. They run like the lightnings.” The chariots are now in the streets and the wide ways, like torches and like lightning. The assault has entered the city’s spaces. The comparisons are speed and fire, and they are not enlarged.

Arminian readers hear streets that are no longer safe, a rushing that the city can no longer keep outside the gates, a word that still describes the crisis as something unfolding in real ways and streets.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the raging chariots, the rush in the wide ways, and the torch-and-lightning appearance as the LORD’s appointed chaos inside the city.

Shared ground: the chariots run in the streets like lightning. The siege language stays with the movement of the chariots.

verses.text: He summons his picked troops. They stumble on their way. They dash to its wall, and the protective shield is put in place.
verses.arminianNotes:
One summons picked troops. They stumble on their way, dash to the wall, and a protective shield is put in place. Readers differ on whether the one who summons is the attacker or Nineveh’s own commander; the verse says they stumble on their way and dash to the wall, and that the protective shield is put in place. The stumbling and the wall are the movement of the line, and they are not turned into a longer scene.

Arminian readers hear troops that do not come on in perfect order, a dash to the wall, and a shield set up, a moment of confusion inside a real assault, still told as a warning to the city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the summoned troops, the stumbling, the dash to the wall, and the protective shield as the unfolding of the judgment already decreed, whoever the summoner is.

Shared ground: picked troops are summoned, they stumble, and they dash to the wall. The verse does not name the one who summons them.

verses.text: The gates of the rivers are opened, and the palace is dissolved.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The gates of the rivers are opened, and the palace is dissolved.” River gates are opened, and the palace dissolves. Many readers take this as water breaking into the city; the verse itself says the gates of the rivers are opened and the palace is dissolved, and it does not describe a later siege in detail.

Arminian readers hear a city’s defenses failing at the water gates, a palace that cannot stand, a word that still treats the end as the LORD’s doing through means the city can picture.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the opened river gates and the dissolved palace as the LORD’s appointed breach, the turning point of the assault.

Shared ground: the river gates are opened, and the palace is dissolved. How later readers have pictured that opening is more than the line itself supplies.

verses.text: It is decreed: she is uncovered, she is carried away; and her servants moan as with the voice of doves, beating on their breasts.
verses.arminianNotes:
“It is decreed: she is uncovered, she is carried away; and her servants moan as with the voice of doves, beating on their breasts.” The decree is exile and exposure: she is uncovered and carried away, and the servants moan like doves, beating on their breasts. The mourning is named in that sound and gesture, and the uncovering is told in one word, without further description.

Arminian readers hear a decreed carrying away, a city’s servants already in mourning, a sentence that is as human as it is final, and still a word spoken before the end has finished.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the decree, the uncovering and carrying away, and the moaning of the servants as the LORD’s appointed end of the city’s self-confidence.

Shared ground: it is decreed, and she is carried away. The servants’ moan is the verse’s own measure of the loss.
